extraction_notes.note: The introduction's summary lists, the proof-strategy subsection 1.4 and the section roadmap are expository and were not extracted; set-up sentences repeated later (e.g. 'Following Definition ..., let S be a set of normal representatives' in 3.2, the polarization/Weil representation set-up in 3.1) were folded into the first statement or skipped.
Section 4.1 contains a table summarizing in which (E/F, K/F) cases the fundamental lemma and smooth transfer are proved; it has no node, its content is carried by the propositions of 4.2-4.4.
Labelled item of a custom 'num' list (equation-numbered) stating an implication; typed claim rather than equation, with the following 'Indeed' paragraph as its proof.
Global reduction formula is a standard consequence of Poisson summation, stated as Theorem with a one-line justification; kept origin paper with rigor semi_formal rather than external.
The sentence 'From Lemma ..., we have' runs straight into the lemma environment with no colon; taken as a one-sentence prose proof of that lemma.

The main theorem's two directions are proved by two separate proof environments; no other node uses a single direction, so both proofs carry a proves edge to the theorem instead of splitting it into claims.

The main theorem is a restatable environment re-printed as \mainthm* in Section 6.2 (recorded in also_stated_at); one sentence in 4.2 ('Note that ... is fixed by ...') has no terminal period and was not extracted.

nodes.name: Adelic quotient [G]
nodes.statement: Denote by $[G]=G(F) \backslash G(\mathbb A)$ the adelic quotient with suitable Haar measure.
nodes.section: 1.1 Relative trace formulas in polarized reductive cases

nodes.name: Period integral P_X
nodes.statement: We define the period integral $P_X(\varphi) = \int_{[G]} \varphi(h) dh$ for $\varphi \in \pi$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Relative trace formulas in polarized reductive cases

nodes.name: Relative trace formula RTF_X
nodes.statement:
Consider the relative trace formula
\[
\mathrm{RTF}_{X}(f):= \int_{[H] \times [H]} K_f(h_1, h_2)  dh _1 dh_2, \quad f \in \mathcal{S}(G(\mathbb A)).
\]\
Here $K_f(x, y)=\sum_{\gamma \in G(F)} f(x^{-1}\gamma y)$ is the kernel function on $[G] \times [G]$ for the right translation action $R(f)$ on the spectrum $L^2([G])$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Relative trace formulas in polarized reductive cases
nodes.statement_short: The relative trace formula is the double integral over [H]x[H] of the automorphic kernel K_f.

nodes.name: Cuspidal kernel K_{f,pi}
nodes.statement:
When the center of $G$ is anistropic, the kernel function for $R(f)$ on $\pi \subseteq L^2_{\mathrm{cusp}}([G])$ is 
\[
K_{f,\pi}(x,y)= \sum_{\phi \in \mathrm{OB}(\pi)} (R(f)\phi(x)) \overline{\phi(y)}
\]
where $\mathrm{OB}(\pi)$ is an orthonormal basis of $\pi$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Relative trace formulas in polarized reductive cases

nodes.name: Spectral piece RTF_{X,pi}
nodes.statement:
Then
\[
\mathrm{RTF}_{X,\pi}(f):= \int_{[H] \times [H]} K_{f,\pi}(h_1, h_2)  dh_1 dh_2 = \sum_{\phi \in \mathrm{OB}(\pi)} P_X(R(f)\phi) \overline{P_X(\phi)}
\]
is directly related to the non-vanishing of $P_X$ on $\pi$, and appear as a direct summand of $\mathrm{RTF}_{X}(f)$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Relative trace formulas in polarized reductive cases
nodes.statement_short: The pi-part of RTF_X equals a sum of products of period integrals P_X over an orthonormal basis of pi.

nodes.name: Geometric decomposition of RTF_X into orbital integrals
nodes.statement:
The key for the relative trace formula approach is a geometric decomposition of the relative trace formula into orbital integrals (for a good test function $f$ with regular support)
\[
\mathrm{RTF}_{X}(f)=\sum_{\gamma \in [H(F)\backslash G(F) / H(F)]_{rs}} \mathrm{Vol}([(H \times H)_\gamma]) \mathrm{Orb}(\gamma, f)
\]
where we consider orbits and orbital integrals for the natural action of $H \times H$ on $G$. And $\mathrm{Vol}([(H \times H)_\gamma])$ is the volume of adelic quotient of the stabilizer $(H \times H)_\gamma$ over $F$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Relative trace formulas in polarized reductive cases
nodes.statement_short: For good test functions RTF_X(f) is a sum over regular semisimple double cosets of volumes times orbital integrals.

nodes.name: Factorization of global orbital integrals
nodes.statement:
When $f=\otimes_v f_v$ is a pure tensor and the stabilizer of $\gamma$ is trivial, we have a decomposition:
\[
\mathrm{Orb}(\gamma, f)= \prod_v \mathrm{Orb}_v(\gamma, f_v)
\]
where $v$ runs over all places of $F$, $\mathrm{Orb}_v(\gamma, f_v)=\int_{(H \times H)(F_v)} f_v(h_1^{-1} \gamma h_2) dh_1 dh_2$ is the local orbital integral at $v$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Relative trace formulas in polarized reductive cases
conclusions: \mathrm{Orb}(\gamma, f)= \prod_v \mathrm{Orb}_v(\gamma, f_v)

nodes.name: Hermitian cuspidal representation
nodes.section: 1.2 Results on the twisted GGP conjecture
differentia: The Asai $L$-function $L(s,\Pi,\operatorname{As}_{L/K}^{(-1)^{n+1}})$ has a pole at $s=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Pi is Hermitian if it is conjugate self-dual and its Asai L-function for L/K of sign (-1)^{n+1} has a pole at s=1.

nodes.name: Nearly equivalent representations
nodes.statement:
In general, suppose $V$ and $V'$ are two skew-Hermitian spaces of dimension $n$ over $E$. For almost all places $v$
of $F$, we have $\mathrm{U}(V)(K_v) \simeq \mathrm{U}(V')(K_v)$. We say that a representation
$\pi$ of $\mathrm{U}(V)(\mathbb A_K)$ and a representation
$\pi'$ of $\mathrm{U}(V')(\mathbb A_K)$ are \emph{nearly equivalent}
if $\pi_v \simeq \pi_v'$ for all but finitely many
places $v$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Results on the twisted GGP conjecture

nodes.name: Equal weak base change implies near equivalence
nodes.statement:
If the weak base change of $\pi$ and $\pi'$ to $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb A_L)$ agree, 
$\pi$ and $\pi'$ are nearly equivalent.
nodes.section: 1.2 Results on the twisted GGP conjecture
assumptions: the weak base change of $\pi$ and $\pi'$ to $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb A_L)$ agree
conclusions: $\pi$ and $\pi'$ are nearly equivalent

nodes.name: Global twisted Gan--Gross--Prasad conjecture
nodes.statement: We prove the global twisted GGP conjecture \cite{TwistedGGP} under some local assumptions, which says that the non-vanishing of $L(\frac12, \pi, \mathrm{As}_{L/E} \otimes \mu^{-1})$ is equivalent to the non-vanishing of above period integral $\mathcal{P}$ on some $\pi'$ that is nearly equivalent to $\pi$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Results on the twisted GGP conjecture
conclusions: the non-vanishing of $L(\frac12, \pi, \mathrm{As}_{L/E} \otimes \mu^{-1})$ is equivalent to the non-vanishing of above period integral $\mathcal{P}$ on some $\pi'$ that is nearly equivalent to $\pi$
equivalent_conditions: the non-vanishing of above period integral $\mathcal{P}$ on some $\pi'$ that is nearly equivalent to $\pi$
nodes.statement_short: Central Asai L-value L(1/2, pi, As x mu^{-1}) is nonzero iff the theta-twisted unitary period is nonzero on some nearly equivalent pi'.

nodes.name: Spl, Inert, Ram sets of places
nodes.statement: For any extension $L_1/L_2$ of number fields, we denote by $\mathrm{Spl}(L_1/L_2)$, $\mathrm{Inert}(L_1/L_2)$, $\mathrm{Ram}(L_1/L_2)$ the set of finite places of $L_2$ which is completely split, inert, ramified in $L_1$ respectively.
nodes.section: 1.2 Results on the twisted GGP conjecture

nodes.name: Ramification set Ram_F(Pi)
nodes.statement: Let $\mathrm{Ram}_F(\Pi)$ be the set of finite place $v$ of $F$ where $\Pi$ is ramified at some place of $L$ above $v$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Results on the twisted GGP conjecture

nodes.name: Twisted GGP conjecture for Asai L-functions (main theorem)
nodes.statement:
Assume that
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\mathrm{Ram}(E/F) \subseteq \mathrm{Spl}(K/F)$, $\mathrm{Ram}(K/F) \subseteq \mathrm{Spl}(E/F)$.
    \item For $v \in \mathrm{Inert}(E/F) \cap \mathrm{Inert}(K/F)$, $\mu_v$, $\psi_{v}$ are unramified 
    and $j \in \mathcal O_{E,v}^\times$.
    \item Any archimedean and $2$-adic place of $F$ is split in $L$.
    \item $\mathrm{Ram}_F(\Pi) \cap \mathrm{Inert}(E/F) \cap \mathrm{Inert}(K/F) = \emptyset$.
    \item There exist $v_1 \in \mathrm{Spl}(E/F), v_2 \in \mathrm{Spl}(L/F)$ such that $\Pi$ is supercuspidal at all places above $v_1$ and $v_2$.
\end{enumerate}
Then the following are equivalent as predicted by \cite{TwistedGGP}:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The Asai $L$-value $L(\frac 12,\Pi,\operatorname{As}_{L/E} \times \mu^{-1}) \ne 0$.
    
    \item There exists a skew-Hermitian space $V$ of
    dimension $n$ over $E$, and a cuspidal automorphic 
    representation $\pi$ of $\mathrm{U}(V)(\mathbb A_K)$ such that $\operatorname{BC}(\pi) = \Pi$, and the period
    integral  $\mathcal P(f,\phi) = \int_{[\mathrm{U}(V)]}
         f(h)\overline{\Theta(h,\phi)}\, dh\ne 0$
for some $f \in \pi$, $\phi \in \mathcal S(\mathbb L(\mathbb A))$.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 1.2 Results on the twisted GGP conjecture
assumptions: Let $\Pi$ be a Hermitian cuspidal tempered automorphic representation of $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb A_L)$.
Any archimedean and $2$-adic place of $F$ is split in $L$.
There exist $v_1 \in \mathrm{Spl}(E/F), v_2 \in \mathrm{Spl}(L/F)$ such that $\Pi$ is supercuspidal at all places above $v_1$ and $v_2$.
conclusions:
Then the following are equivalent as predicted by \cite{TwistedGGP}:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item The Asai $L$-value $L(\frac 12,\Pi,\operatorname{As}_{L/E} \times \mu^{-1}) \ne 0$.
    
    \item There exists a skew-Hermitian space $V$ of
    dimension $n$ over $E$, and a cuspidal automorphic 
    representation $\pi$ of $\mathrm{U}(V)(\mathbb A_K)$ such that $\operatorname{BC}(\pi) = \Pi$, and the period
    integral  $\mathcal P(f,\phi) = \int_{[\mathrm{U}(V)]}
         f(h)\overline{\Theta(h,\phi)}\, dh\ne 0$
for some $f \in \pi$, $\phi \in \mathcal S(\mathbb L(\mathbb A))$.
equivalent_conditions: There exists a skew-Hermitian space $V$ of dimension $n$ over $E$, and a cuspidal automorphic representation $\pi$ of $\mathrm{U}(V)(\mathbb A_K)$ such that $\operatorname{BC}(\pi) = \Pi$, and the period integral $\mathcal P(f,\phi) = \int_{[\mathrm{U}(V)]} f(h)\overline{\Theta(h,\phi)}\, dh\ne 0$ for some $f \in \pi$, $\phi \in \mathcal S(\mathbb L(\mathbb A))$.
nodes.statement_short: Under local splitting/unramifiedness and two supercuspidal places, L(1/2, Pi, As_{L/E} x mu^{-1}) != 0 iff some U(V) period with theta series is nonzero on a pi with BC(pi)=Pi.
nodes.label: thm:mainthm

nodes.name: Infinitely many admissible K
nodes.statement: If $E/F$ is fixed with split $2$-adic places and archimedean places, under a suitable choice of $\psi$ and $\mu$, we can find infinitely many examples of such $K$ satisfying $(1)(2)(3)$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Results on the twisted GGP conjecture
assumptions: $E/F$ is fixed with split $2$-adic places and archimedean places
under a suitable choice of $\psi$ and $\mu$
conclusions: we can find infinitely many examples of such $K$ satisfying $(1)(2)(3)$

nodes.name: Asai decomposition of base-change Galois representation
nodes.statement:
We have an isomorphism of Galois representations 
\[
\operatorname{As}_{L/E}(\rho|_{L}) \cong \mathrm{Sym}^2 \rho \oplus (\wedge^2 \rho \otimes \eta_{L/E}),
\]
where $\eta_{L/E}$ is the quadratic Hecke character of $E$ associated to $L/E$ by global class field theory.
conclusions: \operatorname{As}_{L/E}(\rho|_{L}) \cong \mathrm{Sym}^2 \rho \oplus (\wedge^2 \rho \otimes \eta_{L/E})
nodes.statement_short: Asai of a restricted Galois representation splits as Sym^2 rho plus wedge^2 rho twisted by eta_{L/E}.

nodes.name: Smooth transfer for all test functions at every place
nodes.statement: It is important to prove the existence of smooth transfers for all test functions at any place, which would in particular remove local assumptions (1)(3) in Theorem \ref{thm:mainthm}.
nodes.section: 1.5 Further applications and relative Langlands program
nodes.statement_short: Prove existence of smooth transfer for all test functions at all places, removing local assumptions (1),(3) of the main theorem.

nodes.name: Tuple (G,H,rho,0) and its Weil representation
nodes.statement: Besides Whittaker and non-reductive cases, period integrals in \cite{BZSV, MWZ24} are constructed from a tuple $(G, H, \rho, 0)$: here $H \leq G$ is a reductive subgroup and $\rho: H \to \mathrm{Sp}(V)$ is a symplectic representation which induces a Weil representation $\omega$ of $H$ on $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb L(\mathbb A))$ where $\mathbb L$ is a Langragian of $V$.
nodes.section: 1.5 Further applications and relative Langlands program

nodes.name: rho-theta series Theta_L
nodes.statement:
For $\phi \in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb L(\mathbb A))$, we have the $\rho$-theta series on $[H]$
\[
\Theta_{\mathbb L}(h, \phi)=\sum_{x \in \mathbb L(F)}  \omega(h)\phi(x).
\]
nodes.section: 1.5 Further applications and relative Langlands program

nodes.name: Period integral P_{(G,H,rho)}
nodes.statement:
For a cuspidal automorphic form $\varphi$ on $G(\mathbb A)$, consider its period integral (we use complex conjugation following \cite[Section 2.2]{TwistedGGP})
\[
P_{(G, H, \rho)}(\varphi, \phi)=\int_{[H]} \varphi(h) \overline{\Theta_{\mathbb L}(h, \phi)} dh.
\]
nodes.section: 1.5 Further applications and relative Langlands program

nodes.name: Relative trace formula RTF_{(G,H,rho)}
nodes.statement:
The relative trace formula on $f \in \mathcal{S}(G(\mathbb A)), \phi_1, \phi_2 \in \mathcal{S}(\mathbb L(\mathbb A))$ is 
\[
\mathrm{RTF}_{(G, H,\rho)}(f, \phi_1, \phi_2):= \int_{[H] \times [H]} \sum_{\gamma \in G(F)} f(h_1^{-1}\gamma h_2) \overline{\Theta_{\mathbb L}(h_1, \phi_1)} \Theta_{\mathbb L}(h_2, \phi_2) dh_1 dh_2,
\]
which is related to period integrals via the spectral decomposition:
\[
\mathrm{RTF}_{(G, H,\rho)}(f, \phi_1, \phi_2)=\sum_{\pi} \sum_{\varphi \in OB(\pi)} P_{(G,H,\rho)}(R(f)\varphi, \phi_1) \overline{P_{(G,H,\rho)}(\varphi, \overline{\phi}_2)}.
\]
nodes.section: 1.5 Further applications and relative Langlands program
nodes.statement_short: RTF for (G,H,rho): integrate the kernel against two rho-theta series; spectrally a sum of products of periods.

nodes.name: Relative trace formula RTF_{(G',H_1,rho_1,H_2)}
nodes.statement:
Similarly, consider a pair $(G', H_1, \rho_1)$ and a reductive subgroup $H_2 \leq G'$ and form a relative trace formula
\[
\mathrm{RTF}_{(G', H_1, \rho_1, H_2)}(f', \phi_1'):= \int_{[H_1] \times [H_2]} \sum_{\gamma \in G(F)} f'(h_1^{-1}\gamma h_2) \Theta_{\mathbb L'}(h_1, \phi_1') dh_1 dh_2.
\]
nodes.section: 1.5 Further applications and relative Langlands program

nodes.name: Semisimple and regular elements
nodes.statement: And $x \in X$ is called semisimple if $G.x$ is closed, and regular if the stabilizer $G_x$ has minimal dimension among all orbits.

nodes.name: Quadratic extension E/F
nodes.statement: Let $E/F$ be a quadratic extension of number fields.

nodes.name: Galois generator sigma_{E/F}
nodes.statement: Denote by $\sigma_{E/F}$ the generator of $\mathrm{Gal}(E/F)$.

nodes.name: Totally imaginary elements j and j_M
nodes.statement: We use $j \in E$ (resp. $j_M \in M$) to be a totally imaginary element in $E/F$ (resp. $M/F$).

nodes.name: Skew-hermitian space
nodes.statement:
By a skew-hermitian space $V$ over $E$, we mean a 
$E$-vector space $V$ equipped with an skew-Hermitian form $\left<-,-\right>: V \times V \to E$, 
i.e. it is $\sigma_{E/F}$-linear in the first variable, 
linear in the second variable, and 
$\left<x,y\right>=-\sigma_{E/F}(\left<y,x\right>)$.
differentia: equipped with an skew-Hermitian form $\left<-,-\right>: V \times V \to E$

nodes.name: Isomorphism classes [SHerm_n^x(F)]
nodes.statement:
Let $[\mathrm{SHerm}_n^\times(F)]$ denote the set
of isomorphism classes of $n$-dimensional
nondegenerate skew-Hermitian spaces over $E$.

nodes.name: Quadratic character eta_{E/F} and character mu
nodes.statement:
Let $\eta_{E/F}$ be the quadratic character of
$\mathbb A^\times/F^\times$ associated to $E/F$ by
global class field theory, and $\mu$ be a character
of $\mathbb A_E^\times/E^\times$ such that 
$\mu|_{\mathbb A^\times} = \eta_{E/F}$.

nodes.name: Quadratic character eta_{L/K}
nodes.statement: Similarly, we denote by $\eta_{L/K}$ the quadratic character of $\mathbb A^\times_K$ associated to $L/K$.

nodes.name: Additive characters psi and psi_E
nodes.statement: Let $\psi: \mathbb A_F / F \to \mathbb C^\times$ be a non-trivial additive character, which gives a character $\psi_E(x)=\psi(\mathrm{Tr}_{E/F}(x)): \mathbb A_E / E \to \mathbb C^\times$.

nodes.name: Quadratic extension K/F
nodes.statement: Let $K/F$ be another quadratic extension of number fields.

nodes.name: Galois generator sigma_{K/F}
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma_{K/F}$ be the generator of $\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$.

nodes.name: Groups H, G, H_1, G', H_2
nodes.statement:
Set 
$$
H=\mathrm{U}(V) \to G=\mathrm{Res}_{K/F}\mathrm{U}(V_K),
$$
\[
H_1 = \mathrm{Res}_{E/F} \mathrm{GL}_n, \quad G' = \mathrm{Res}_{L/F} \mathrm{GL}_n, \quad H_2 = \mathrm{Res}_{K/F} \mathrm{GL}_n.
\]

nodes.name: Third quadratic subfield M
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be the subfield of $L$ fixed by $\sigma_{L/K} \circ \sigma_{L/E}$.

nodes.name: Element j_M
nodes.statement:
We fix an element $j_M \in M$ satisfying 
$\sigma_{M/F}(j_M) = - j_M$.

nodes.name: Character eta'
nodes.statement: We choose $\eta'$ a character of $\mathbb A^\times_L$ such that $\eta'|_{\mathbb A^\times_K}=\eta_{L/K}$.

nodes.name: Split central component A_G^infty
nodes.statement: For any connected reductive group $G$ over a number field $F$, let $A_G^\infty$ be the connected component of the $\mathbb R$-point of the split center of the $\mathbb Q$-group $\mathrm{Res}_{F/\mathbb Q} G$.

nodes.name: Tamagawa measure and constant Delta_G^*
nodes.statement: The Tamagawa measure $dg$ on $G(\mathbb A_F)$ is of the form $dg = (\Delta_G^*)^{-1} \prod dg_v$, where $dg_v$ is a Haar measure on $G(F_v)$ such that the hyperspecial subgroup has Haar measure 1 for almost all $v$ and $\Delta_G^*$ is a constant.

nodes.name: Stabilizer in the diagonal for torus centralizers
nodes.statement: Given $\zeta \in G$, if the centralizer $C_G(\theta(\zeta^{-1})\zeta)$ of $\theta(\zeta^{-1}) \zeta$ in $G$ is a torus and $\zeta \in C_G(\theta(\zeta^{-1})\zeta)$, then $H \times H$-stabilizer of $\zeta$ is in the diagonal subgroup $H \leq H \times H$.
assumptions: the centralizer $C_G(\theta(\zeta^{-1})\zeta)$ of $\theta(\zeta^{-1}) \zeta$ in $G$ is a torus
conclusions: $H \times H$-stabilizer of $\zeta$ is in the diagonal subgroup $H \leq H \times H$

nodes.name: Proof of the diagonal-stabilizer claim
nodes.statement: Indeed, under the assumption, we have $C(\theta(\zeta)^{-1}\zeta) \subseteq C(\zeta)$. Note that $g^{-1}\zeta h =\zeta$ for $g, h \in H$ implies that $g^{-1}\theta(\zeta) h =\theta(\zeta)$, hence $h^{-1} \zeta^{-1} \theta(\zeta) h= \zeta^{-1} \theta(\zeta)$, hence $h \in C(\theta(\zeta)^{-1}\zeta)$.
nodes.statement_short: Direct: a stabilizing pair (g,h) forces h into the centralizer of theta(zeta)^{-1}zeta, which lies in C(zeta).

nodes.name: T_0-good element
nodes.statement: Consider the action of a group $T$ on a set $S$, with a subgroup $T_0 \leq T$. Our interest is on the locus of $x \in S$ such that $\mathrm{Stab}_{T}(x) \leq T_0$, which is stable under the action of $T_0$. We call such $x$ a $T_0$-good element in $S$.

nodes.name: Orbit bijection from a transversal subset
assumptions: For any $\widetilde{y} \in \widetilde{S}$, there exists $y \in S$ and $g \in T$ such that $g\widetilde{y}=y$.
If $gy_1=y_2$ for some $g \in T$ and $y_1, y_2 \in S$, then there exists $h \in H$ such that $hy_1=y_2$.
conclusions: the natural inclusion $H \backslash S \to G \backslash \widetilde{S}$ is a bijection

nodes.name: Commuting involutions theta_1, theta_2 and fixed subgroups
nodes.statement:
Let $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ be commuting
involutions of $G$,
and let $H_1$ and $H_2$ be the subgroups of $G$ fixed
by $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$, respectively.

nodes.name: Antisymmetric locus G^{theta_2=(-)^{-1}}
nodes.statement:
We have a $H_1$-equivariant embedding 
\[
G/H_2 \hookrightarrow G,  \, \, \xi \mapsto \gamma=\xi \theta_2(\xi)^{-1}
\]
whose image lies in $G^{\theta_2=(-)^{-1}}:=\{ \gamma \in G : \gamma \theta_2(\gamma)=1\}$. Here $H_1$ acts on $\gamma \in G^{\theta_2=(-)^{-1}}$ by
\[
    \gamma.h_1 = h_1^{-1}\gamma \theta_2(h_1).
\]

$\gamma$ commutes with $\theta_1\theta_2(\gamma) = \theta_1(\gamma)^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Normal elements are good
nodes.statement:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item An element $\gamma$ is normal iff $\theta_1 \theta_2(\delta)=\delta$.
    \item If $\gamma$ is $\theta_1\theta_2$-normal and
the centralizer $C_G(\delta)$ is a
torus in $G$, then $\mathrm{Stab}_{H_1}(\gamma) \subseteq H_1^{\theta_2=\mathrm{id}}$.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, if $\delta$ is regular semisimple and $C_G(\delta)$ is a torus and $\gamma$ is $\theta_1\theta_2$-normal, then $\delta$ is good.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.1.3
nodes.statement:
The first part follows from the definition. Suppose $h \in H_1$ satisfies $h^{-1}\gamma \theta_2(h)
= \gamma$. Then 
\[
    \theta_2(h)^{-1}\theta_1\theta_2(\gamma)
    h = \theta_1\theta_2(\gamma),
\]
so $h \in C_G(\gamma\theta_1\theta_2(\gamma))$.
By assumption 
$\gamma \in C_G(\gamma\theta_1\theta_2(\gamma))$
as well, so $\gamma$ and $h$ commute.
This combined with $h^{-1}\gamma \theta_2(h) 
= \gamma$ implies that $h = \theta_2(h)$ as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Direct: a stabilizer h centralizes gamma*theta1theta2(gamma); normality makes gamma commute with h, forcing h = theta_2(h).

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.2.3

$$

If $\zeta$ is good, then $h^{-1}\zeta h$ is also good for any $h \in H$ by definition.

nodes.name: Normal representatives R and [Y_rss] (unitary side)
nodes.statement:
Choose a set $R$ of normal representatives of
the regular semisimple $H(F) \times H(F)$-orbits
of $G(F)$ that contain a normal element. Let 
\[
    Y =R^V\times V^\vee.
\]
For $\zeta \in R^V$, consider the action of $T_\zeta \subseteq H$ on $z \in V^\vee$ by right multiplication.  We say that $z$ is regular semisimple if it is under the action of $T_\zeta$.  Let $(R^V\times V^\vee)_{\textnormal{rss}}$ be the set of elements of $Y$ such that $z$ is regular semisimple. 

Form the equivalence relation 
$[\zeta, z] \sim [\zeta, zt]$ for $t \in T_\zeta$ on $(R^V\times V^\vee)_{\textnormal{rss}}$. Let 
\begin{equation}
[Y_{\textnormal{rss}}]=(R^V\times V^\vee)_{\textnormal{rss}} / \sim
\end{equation}
be the set of regular semisimple equivalence classes.

Note that $H$ acts on $G_{\textnormal{good}} \times V \subseteq G \times V$, and we could consider orbital integrals for this restricted action. nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.3.3
nodes.statement:
This follows from the fact that for any $h_1 \in H_1(F)$, 
there exist $h_2 \in H_2(F)$ such that
$(h_1, h_2) \in T'_\xi$ if and only if $h_1 \in T_\gamma$.
Indeed, if $(h_1, h_2) \in T_\xi'$, then 
\[
    \gamma = \xi \sigma_{L/K}(\xi)^{-1}
    = (h_1^{-1} \xi h_2)(h_2^{-1} \sigma_{L/K}(\xi)^{-1} \sigma_{E/F}(h_1))
    = h_1^{-1} \gamma \sigma_{E/F}(h_1),
\]
so $h_1 \in T_\gamma$. On the other hand, if $h_1 \in T_\gamma$,
then $(h_1, h_2) \in T_\xi'$ for $h_2 = \xi^{-1}h_1\xi$, which
is an element of $H_2(F)$ since
\[
    \sigma_{L/K}(h_2) = \sigma_{L/K}(\xi)^{-1} \sigma_{E/F}(h_1)
    \sigma_{L/K}(\xi) = \xi^{-1} h_1 \xi = h_2,
\] 
where the middle equality follows from $h_1 \in T_\gamma$.

nodes.statement_short: Show h_1 extends to a stabilizing pair iff h_1 in T_gamma, by direct computation in both directions.

nodes.name: Cayley transform c_alpha
nodes.statement:
For any $\alpha \in L^\times$, let 
\[
D_\alpha = \{x \in \mathfrak{gl}_n(L) : \det(\alpha - x) = 0 \}. 
\]
The Cayley transform is the map
\begin{align*}
    c_\alpha \colon \mathfrak{gl}_n(L) - D_\alpha &\xrightarrow{\raisebox{-0.7ex}[0ex][0ex]{$\sim$}} \mathfrak{gl}_n(L) - D_1 \\
    \delta &\mapsto - (\alpha + \delta )(\alpha - \delta)^{-1},
\end{align*}
which has inverse $c_\alpha^{-1}(x) = -\alpha(1 + x)(1 - x)^{-1}$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Normal representatives on the base change side
nodes.statement_short: c_alpha(delta) = -(alpha+delta)(alpha-delta)^{-1}, a bijection away from the loci D_alpha and D_1.

nodes.name: Cayley transform restricts to symmetric spaces
nodes.statement:
The Cayley transform is $G'$-equivariant, and
if $\alpha \sigma_{L/E}(\alpha) = 1$, it induces an isomorphism
\[
    c_\alpha \colon \textnormal{S}_{n, L/E} - D_\alpha \xrightarrow{\raisebox{-0.7ex}[0ex][0ex]{$\sim$}} \mathfrak s_{n, L/E} - D_1.
\]
If $\alpha\sigma_{L/K}(\alpha) = 1$, it induces
isomorphisms
\[
    c_\alpha \colon \textnormal{S}_{n, L/K} - D_\alpha \xrightarrow{\raisebox{-0.7ex}[0ex][0ex]{$\sim$}}
    \mathfrak s_{n, L/K} - D_1,
\]
\[
    c_\alpha \colon \mathrm{U}(V_K) - D_\alpha \xrightarrow{\raisebox{-0.7ex}[0ex][0ex]{$\sim$}}
    \mathfrak u(V_K) - D_1.
\]
nodes.section: 2.3 Normal representatives on the base change side
nodes.statement_short: c_alpha is G'-equivariant and identifies S_{n,L/E}, S_{n,L/K}, U(V_K) (minus D_alpha) with their Lie algebras (minus D_1).

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.3.8
nodes.statement:
We want to show that there exists
$g \in H_1$ such that 
$g^{-1}\delta g \in \mathrm{GL}_n(M)$, since
for such $g$, the element $\gamma.g$ would be normal,
since
\[
    (\gamma.g)\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma.g)^{-1}
    = g^{-1}\delta g
\]
by \eqref{eq:norm}.

It is clear that $\delta$ is an element of $\textnormal{S}_{n, L/E}$.
Let $\alpha \in M$ be such that
$\alpha \sigma_{M/F}(\alpha) = 1$ and $\alpha$ is not
an eigenvalue of $\delta$. Let $A = j_M c_\alpha(\delta)$.
We have $c_\alpha(\delta) \in \mathfrak s_{n, L/E}$, so $A \in \mathrm{Mat}_n(E)$.

Note that 
\[
    \sigma_{L/M}(\delta) = 
    \sigma_{L/E}\circ \sigma_{L/K}(\gamma)\sigma_{L/K}(\gamma)^{-1}
    = \sigma_{L/E}(\gamma)^{-1} \gamma
    = \gamma^{-1} \delta \gamma.
\]
Since $\sigma_{L/M}(\alpha) = \alpha$, we also have
\begin{align*}
    c_\alpha(\sigma_{L/M}(\delta))
    &= - (\alpha + \sigma_{L/M}(\delta))(\alpha - \sigma_{L/M}(\delta))^{-1}\\
    &= \sigma_{L/M}(-(\alpha + \delta)(\alpha - \delta)^{-1}) = \sigma_{L/M}(c_\alpha(\delta)).
\end{align*}
Combining the previous two displayed equations, we obtain
\[
    \sigma_{L/M}(c_\alpha(\delta)) = \gamma c_\alpha(\delta) \gamma^{-1}.
\]
Since $A = j_M c_\alpha(\delta)$ and $j_M \in M$, 
this implies
\[
    \sigma_{E/F}(A) = \sigma_{L/M}(A) = \gamma^{-1} A \gamma.
\]

This implies that the elementary divisors of
$A$ have coefficients in $F$, so there exists $g \in H_1$ such
that $g^{-1} A g \in \mathfrak{gl}_n(F)$. Now we can transform it back using Cayley maps.

This means $g^{-1} c_\alpha(\delta) g \in \mathfrak{gl}_n(M)$, so 
\[
    g^{-1}\delta g = c_\alpha^{-1}(g^{-1} c_\alpha(\delta) g) \in \mathrm{GL}_n(M). \qedhere
\]
nodes.section: 2.3 Normal representatives on the base change side
nodes.statement_short: Cayley-transform the norm delta to a matrix A over E with sigma(A) conjugate to A, then descend A to gl_n(F) and transform back.

nodes.name: Pick alpha in M of norm 1 not an eigenvalue; set A = j_M c_a
nodes.statement:
It is clear that $\delta$ is an element of $\textnormal{S}_{n, L/E}$.
Let $\alpha \in M$ be such that
$\alpha \sigma_{M/F}(\alpha) = 1$ and $\alpha$ is not
an eigenvalue of $\delta$. Let $A = j_M c_\alpha(\delta)$.
We have $c_\alpha(\delta) \in \mathfrak s_{n, L/E}$, so $A \in \mathrm{Mat}_n(E)$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick alpha in M of norm 1 not an eigenvalue; set A = j_M c_alpha(delta) in Mat_n(E).
nodes.section: 2.3 Normal representatives on the base change side

nodes.name: Compute sigma_{L/M} on delta and on c_alpha(delta): sigma_{E
nodes.statement:
Note that 
\[
    \sigma_{L/M}(\delta) = 
    \sigma_{L/E}\circ \sigma_{L/K}(\gamma)\sigma_{L/K}(\gamma)^{-1}
    = \sigma_{L/E}(\gamma)^{-1} \gamma
    = \gamma^{-1} \delta \gamma.
\]
Since $\sigma_{L/M}(\alpha) = \alpha$, we also have
\begin{align*}
    c_\alpha(\sigma_{L/M}(\delta))
    &= - (\alpha + \sigma_{L/M}(\delta))(\alpha - \sigma_{L/M}(\delta))^{-1}\\
    &= \sigma_{L/M}(-(\alpha + \delta)(\alpha - \delta)^{-1}) = \sigma_{L/M}(c_\alpha(\delta)).
\end{align*}
Combining the previous two displayed equations, we obtain
\[
    \sigma_{L/M}(c_\alpha(\delta)) = \gamma c_\alpha(\delta) \gamma^{-1}.
\]
Since $A = j_M c_\alpha(\delta)$ and $j_M \in M$, 
this implies
\[
    \sigma_{E/F}(A) = \sigma_{L/M}(A) = \gamma^{-1} A \gamma.
\]
nodes.statement_short: Compute sigma_{L/M} on delta and on c_alpha(delta): sigma_{E/F}(A) = gamma^{-1} A gamma.
nodes.section: 2.3 Normal representatives on the base change side

nodes.name: Elementary divisors of A are over F, so A is H_1-conjugate i
nodes.statement:
This implies that the elementary divisors of
$A$ have coefficients in $F$, so there exists $g \in H_1$ such
that $g^{-1} A g \in \mathfrak{gl}_n(F)$. Now we can transform it back using Cayley maps.
nodes.statement_short: Elementary divisors of A are over F, so A is H_1-conjugate into gl_n(F).
nodes.section: 2.3 Normal representatives on the base change side

nodes.name: Inverting the Cayley transform puts g^{-1} delta g in GL_n(M
nodes.statement:
This means $g^{-1} c_\alpha(\delta) g \in \mathfrak{gl}_n(M)$, so 
\[
    g^{-1}\delta g = c_\alpha^{-1}(g^{-1} c_\alpha(\delta) g) \in \mathrm{GL}_n(M). \qedhere
\]
nodes.statement_short: Inverting the Cayley transform puts g^{-1} delta g in GL_n(M).
nodes.section: 2.3 Normal representatives on the base change side

nodes.name: Norm determines the H_1-orbit
nodes.statement:
If $\gamma$ and $\gamma'$ are elements of $\textnormal{S}_{n, L/K}$ such that
$\gamma\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma)^{-1}$ and $\gamma'\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma')^{-1}$ are conjugate
by an element of $H_1$, 
then $\gamma$ and $\gamma'$ are in the same $H_1$-orbit
of $\textnormal{S}_{n,L/K}$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Normal representatives on the base change side
assumptions: $\gamma\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma)^{-1}$ and $\gamma'\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma')^{-1}$ are conjugate by an element of $H_1$
conclusions: $\gamma$ and $\gamma'$ are in the same $H_1$-orbit of $\textnormal{S}_{n,L/K}$
nodes.statement_short: Elements of S_{n,L/K} whose norms are H_1-conjugate lie in the same H_1-orbit (cf. Arthur--Clozel).
nodes.label: lem:injnorm

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.3.9
nodes.statement:
By Proposition \ref{prop:normalrep},
we can assume that $\gamma$ and $\gamma'$ are normal
(see Definition \ref{def:glnormal}).
By \eqref{eq:norm}, 
we can assume that $\gamma\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma)^{-1}
= \gamma'\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma')^{-1} = \delta$.

Let
\[
    \mathfrak t_\gamma(F) = \{g \in \mathfrak{gl}_n(E) :
    \gamma \sigma_{E/F}(g) = g\gamma\}.
\]
This is an $F$-algebra. Let 
\[
    \mathfrak t_\gamma(E) = \{g \in \mathfrak{gl}_n(E) :
    \delta g = x \delta \}.
\]

We have an isomorphism
\[
    x \otimes e \mapsto xe\colon  \mathfrak t_\gamma(F)
\otimes_F E \simeq \mathfrak t_\gamma(E).
\]
Indeed, this map is injective because every element
of $\mathfrak t_\gamma(F) \otimes_F E$ is of the
form $g_1 \otimes 1 + g_2 \otimes j_E$, and if
$g_1 + j_Eg_2 = 0$ for 
$g_1, g_2 \in \mathfrak t_\gamma(F)$, then
\[
    \gamma\sigma_{E/F}(g_1)
    = g_1\gamma 
    = -j_Eg_2 \gamma
    = -j_E\gamma\sigma_{E/F}(g_2)
    = - \gamma\sigma_{E/F}(g_1),
\]
so $g_1 = g_2 = 0$.
It is surjective because 
if $g \in \mathfrak t_\gamma(E)$, then
$\gamma \sigma_{E/F}(g) \gamma^{-1} \in \mathrm{Mat}_n(E)$
since
\[
    \sigma_{L/K} \circ \sigma_{L/E}(\gamma \sigma_{E/F}(g) \gamma^{-1})
    = \sigma_{L/E}(\gamma)^{-1} g
    \sigma_{L/E}(\gamma) = \gamma^{-1} g \gamma
    = \sigma_{L/K}(\gamma \sigma_{E/F}(g) \gamma^{-1}),
\]
where we have used the fact that 
$\gamma\sigma_{L/K}(\gamma) = 1$,
and the middle equality holds since $\delta g = g\delta$.
Then
\[
   \sigma_{E/F}(\gamma \sigma_{E/F}(g) \gamma^{-1})
   = \sigma_{L/K}(\gamma \sigma_{E/F}(g) \gamma^{-1})
   = \gamma^{-1} g \gamma,
\]
so
\[
    \gamma \sigma_{E/F}(g + \gamma 
    \sigma_{E/F}(g) \gamma^{-1})
    = \gamma(\sigma_{E/F}(g) + \gamma^{-1} g \gamma)
    = \gamma \sigma_{E/F}(g) + g \gamma
    = (g + \gamma \sigma_{E/F} \gamma^{-1})\gamma,
\]
which means
\[
    g + \gamma \sigma_{E/F}(g)\gamma^{-1} \in \mathfrak t_\gamma(F). 
\]
Similarly, we find
\[
    j_E(g - \gamma \sigma_{E/F}(g) \gamma^{-1}) \in
    \mathfrak t_\gamma(F),
\]
so the map $g \otimes e \mapsto ge$ is surjective since
\[
    g = \frac{1}{2}(g + \gamma \sigma_{E/F}(g) \gamma^{-1})
    + \frac{1}{2j_E} \cdot j_E(g - \gamma \sigma_{E/F}(g)\gamma^{-1}).
\]

Under the isomorphism $\mathfrak t_\gamma(F)
\otimes_F E \simeq \mathfrak t_\gamma(E)$,
the corresponding action of $\mathrm{Gal}(E/F)$ on
$\mathfrak t_\gamma(E)$ is given by
\[
    \sigma_{E/F}.g = \gamma \sigma_{E/F}(g) \gamma^{-1}.
\]
Then by Hilbert's Theorem 90 
\cite[Chapter~X,~Section~1,~Exercise~2]{Serre-local}, 
we have 
\begin{equation} H^1(\mathrm{Gal}(E/F), \mathfrak t_\gamma(E)^\times) = 0.
\end{equation}
This is equivalent to the statement that if
$g \in H_1$ satisfies
\[
    g^{-1}\delta g = \delta, \quad
    g(\gamma \sigma_{E/F}(g) \gamma^{-1}) = 1,
\]
then 
\[
    g = h(\gamma \sigma_{E/F}(h) \gamma^{-1})^{-1}
\]
for some $h \in H_1$ satisfying $h^{-1}\delta h = \delta$.

Now let $g = \gamma'\gamma^{-1}$. Note that
$g \in H_1$. This is because since $\gamma$ and $\gamma'$ are normal, we have
\[
    \sigma_{L/E}(\gamma)^{-1}\gamma
    = \gamma\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma)^{-1} 
    = \gamma'\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma')^{-1}
    = \sigma_{L/E}(\gamma')^{-1}\gamma',
\]
so $\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma'\gamma^{-1})
= \gamma'\gamma^{-1}$. 
We also have 
\[
    g^{-1}\delta g 
    = \gamma\gamma'^{-1}
    (\gamma'\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma')^{-1}) \gamma'\gamma^{-1}
    = \gamma (\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma')^{-1}\gamma')
    \gamma^{-1}
    = \delta.
\]
In addition, since $\gamma\sigma_{L/K}(\gamma) = \gamma'\sigma_{L/K}(\gamma') = 1$,
we have $\sigma_{E/F}(g) = \sigma_{L/K}(g)
= \gamma'^{-1}\gamma$, so
\[
    g(\gamma \sigma_{E/F}(g) \gamma^{-1})
    = \gamma'\gamma^{-1} (\gamma (\gamma'^{-1}\gamma)\gamma^{-1}) = 1.
\]
Then by \eqref{eq:Hone}, there exists 
$h \in H_1$ such that
$\gamma'\gamma^{-1} = h(\gamma \sigma_{E/F}(h) \gamma^{-1})^{-1}$, which is equivalent to
$\gamma' = h \gamma \sigma_{E/F}(h)^{-1}$.
\qedhere

    = \gamma\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma)^{-1} 
    = \gamma'\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma')^{-1}

\]
so $\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma'\gamma^{-1})

nodes.name: Normal representatives S and [X_rss] (general linear side)
nodes.statement:
Let $S$ be a set of normal representatives
of the regular semisimple $H_1$-orbits
of $\textnormal{S}_{n,L/K}$. Let 
\[
    X = S \times F_n \times F^{-,n}.
\]
For $\gamma \in S$, consider the action of $T_\gamma \subseteq H_{10}$ on
$[x, y] \in F_n \times F^{-,n}$ given by
$[x, y].t = [xt, t^{-1} y]$.
We say $[x, y]$ is regular semisimple if it is under this
action of $T_\gamma$.

Let $(S \times F_n \times F^{-,n})_{\textnormal{rss}}$ be the set of elements of $X$
such that $[x, y]$ is regular semisimple. Form the equivalence relation
$[\gamma, x, y] \sim [\gamma, xt, t^{-1}y]$ on $(S \times F_n \times F^{-,n})_{\textnormal{rss}}$ 
for $t \in T_\gamma$.
Let 
\[
    [X_{\textnormal{rss}}] = (S \times F_n \times F^{-,n})_{\textnormal{rss}}/\sim
\]
be the set of regular semisimple equivalence classes.
nodes.section: 2.3 Normal representatives on the base change side
nodes.statement_short: Fix normal representatives S of regular semisimple H_1-orbits on S_{n,L/K}; [X_rss] is triples [gamma,x,y] modulo T_gamma.
nodes.label: normal reps: GL side

nodes.name: GL_n(L)-action on Mat_n(L) x L_n x L^n
nodes.statement:
Consider the right action of $\mathrm{GL}_n(L)$ on 
\[
    \mathrm{Mat}_n(L) \times L_n \times L^n
\] 
given by
\[
    [\xi, x, y].h = [h^{-1}\xi h, xh, h^{-1} y].
\]

nodes.name: Invariants a_i and b_i
nodes.statement:
a_i([\xi, x, y]) = \mathrm{Tr} \wedge^i \xi, \quad
    b_i[\xi, x, y]) = x(\xi^{i-1} y)
nodes.label: eq:invar

nodes.name: Strongly regular semisimple
Strongly regular semisimple orbits are classified by invariants
nodes.statement:
Strongly regular semisimple elements of $\mathrm{Mat}_n(L) \times
L_n \times L^n$
have trivial stabilizers, and two strongly 
regular semisimple
elements are in the same $\mathrm{GL}_n(L)$-orbit if and only
if they have the same invariants.
nodes.origin_citation: Liu 2014, Lemma 5.6; Rallis--Schiffmann 2007, Prop. 6.2 and Thm. 6.1
conclusions: Strongly regular semisimple elements of $\mathrm{Mat}_n(L) \times L_n \times L^n$ have trivial stabilizers
two strongly regular semisimple elements are in the same $\mathrm{GL}_n(L)$-orbit if and only if they have the same invariants

nodes.name: Strongly regular semisimple in S_{n,L/E} x E_n x E^n
nodes.statement:
We also consider the space
\[
    \textnormal{S}_{n, L/E} \times E_n \times E^n
\]
which has right action of $\mathrm{GL}_n(E)$ induced 
by the $\mathrm{GL}_n(L)$-action on $\mathrm{Mat}_n(L) \times L_n \times L^n$.
We say that an element of this space is strongly
regular semisimple
if it is strongly regular semisimple as an element of 
$\mathrm{Mat}_n(L) \times L_n \times L^n$.

nodes.name: Embeddings of X and Y into S_{n,L/E} x E_n x E^n
nodes.statement:
We have embeddings
\[
   [\gamma, x, y] \mapsto [\gamma \sigma_{L/E}(\gamma)^{-1}, x, y] \colon X \to 
   \textnormal{S}_{n, L/E} \times E_n \times E^n
\]
and
\[
    [\zeta, z] \mapsto [\zeta \sigma_{L/E}(\zeta)^{-1}, z, z^\ast] \colon
    Y \to \textnormal{S}_{n, L/E} \times E_n \times E^n
\]
such that an element of $X$ or $Y$ is regular
semisimple if and only if its image is strongly regular
semisimple.
conclusions: an element of $X$ or $Y$ is regular semisimple if and only if its image is strongly regular semisimple

nodes.name: Invariants of [gamma,x,y] and [zeta,z]
nodes.statement:
We define the invariants of an element
$[\gamma, x, y] \in X$ or $[\zeta, z] \in Y$
to be equal to the invariants $a_i$ and $b_i$,
as defined in \eqref{eq:invar}, of
its image under the above embeddings.

nodes.name: GL_n(L)-orbits vs GL_n(E)-orbits
nodes.statement:
Two strongly regular semisimple elements of $[\delta, x, y]$ and
$[\delta', x', y']$ of $\textnormal{S}_{n, L/E} \times E_n
\times E^n$ are in the same $\mathrm{GL}_n(L)$-orbit
if and only if they are in the same $\mathrm{GL}_n(E)$-orbit.
assumptions: Two strongly regular semisimple elements of $[\delta, x, y]$ and $[\delta', x', y']$ of $\textnormal{S}_{n, L/E} \times E_n \times E^n$
conclusions: are in the same $\mathrm{GL}_n(L)$-orbit if and only if they are in the same $\mathrm{GL}_n(E)$-orbit
nodes.label: lem:sv

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.4.4
nodes.statement:
Suppose there exists $h \in \mathrm{GL}_n(L)$ such that
\[
    [\delta, x, y].h = [h^{-1}\delta h, xh, h^{-1} y]
    = [\delta', x', y'].
\]
Since $\delta \sigma_{L/E}(\delta) 
= \delta'\sigma_{L/E}(\delta') = 1$, we have
\begin{align*}
    [\delta, x, y].\sigma_{L/E}(h) 
    &= [\sigma_{L/E}(h)^{-1} \delta \sigma_{L/E}(h), x\sigma_{L/E}(h),
    \sigma_{L/E}(h)^{-1}y]\\
    &= \sigma_{L/E}([h^{-1}\delta^{-1} h, xh, h^{-1}y])\\
    &= \sigma_{L/E}([\delta'^{-1}, x', y']) \\
    &= [\delta', x', y'].
\end{align*}
By the triviality of stabilizers of strongly
regular semisimple elements, we have 
$\sigma_{L/E}(h) = h$, so $h \in \mathrm{GL}_n(E)$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply sigma_{L/E} to the orbit relation; trivial stabilizers force h = sigma(h), so h in GL_n(E).

nodes.name: Take h in GL_n(L) relating the two elements.
nodes.statement:
Suppose there exists $h \in \mathrm{GL}_n(L)$ such that
\[
    [\delta, x, y].h = [h^{-1}\delta h, xh, h^{-1} y]
    = [\delta', x', y'].
\]
nodes.statement_short: Take h in GL_n(L) relating the two elements.

nodes.name: sigma_{L/E}(h) also relates them.
nodes.statement:
Since $\delta \sigma_{L/E}(\delta) 
= \delta'\sigma_{L/E}(\delta') = 1$, we have
\begin{align*}
    [\delta, x, y].\sigma_{L/E}(h) 
    &= [\sigma_{L/E}(h)^{-1} \delta \sigma_{L/E}(h), x\sigma_{L/E}(h),
    \sigma_{L/E}(h)^{-1}y]\\
    &= \sigma_{L/E}([h^{-1}\delta^{-1} h, xh, h^{-1}y])\\
    &= \sigma_{L/E}([\delta'^{-1}, x', y']) \\
    &= [\delta', x', y'].
\end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: sigma_{L/E}(h) also relates them.

nodes.name: Trivial stabilizers force sigma(h)=h.
nodes.statement:
By the triviality of stabilizers of strongly
regular semisimple elements, we have 
$\sigma_{L/E}(h) = h$, so $h \in \mathrm{GL}_n(E)$.
nodes.statement_short: Trivial stabilizers force sigma(h)=h.

nodes.name: Equivalence classes are determined by invariants
nodes.statement:
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item
Two elements $[\gamma, x, y]$ and $[\gamma', x', y']$
of $X_{\textnormal{rss}}$ are equivalent if and only if they
have the same invariants.

\item 
Two elements $[\zeta, z]$ and $[\zeta', z']$ of
$Y_{\textnormal{rss}}^V$ are equivalent if and only if
they have the same invariants.
\end{enumerate}
conclusions: Two elements $[\gamma, x, y]$ and $[\gamma', x', y']$ of $X_{\textnormal{rss}}$ are equivalent if and only if they have the same invariants.
Two elements $[\zeta, z]$ and $[\zeta', z']$ of $Y_{\textnormal{rss}}^V$ are equivalent if and only if they have the same invariants.
Two elements $[\gamma, x, y]$ and $[\gamma', x', y']$ of $X_{\textnormal{rss}}$ are equivalent if and only if they have the same invariants.
Two elements $[\zeta, z]$ and $[\zeta', z']$ of $Y_{\textnormal{rss}}^V$ are equivalent if and only if they have the same invariants.

nodes.label: lem:embed

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.4.5
nodes.statement:
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item
Let $\delta = \gamma\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma)^{-1}$ and
$\delta' = \gamma'\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma')^{-1}$.
Note that $[\gamma, x, y]$ and 
$[\gamma', x', y']$ have the same invariants
if and only if $[\delta, x, y]$ and
$[\delta', x', y']$ are in the same $\mathrm{GL}_n(L)$-orbit, 
and thus by Lemma \ref{lem:sv} in the same 
$\mathrm{GL}_n(E)$-orbit.

The only if direction is straightforward, by the
definition of the equivalence relation of $X$.
For the other direction, suppose 
\[
   [\delta, x, y].h = [h^{-1}\delta h, xh, h^{-1}y] =
   [\delta', x', y']
\]
for $h \in \mathrm{GL}_n(E)$.
By Lemma \ref{lem:injnorm}, we have $\gamma = \gamma'$.

Similarly to the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:sv}, 
since $\delta\sigma_{L/K}(\delta) 
= \delta'\sigma_{L/K}(\delta') = 1$, we have
\begin{align*}
    [\delta, x, y].\sigma_{L/K}(h) 
    &= [\sigma_{L/K}(h)^{-1} \delta \sigma_{L/K}(h), x\sigma_{L/K}(h),
    \sigma_{L/K}(h)^{-1}y]\\
    &= \sigma_{L/K}([h^{-1}\delta^{-1} h, xh, -h^{-1}y])\\
    &= \sigma_{L/K}([\delta'^{-1}, x', -y']) \\
    &= [\delta', x', y'].
\end{align*}
By triviality of stabilizers, we have $\sigma_{L/K}(h) = h$,
so $h \in \mathrm{GL}_n(F)$. 
Since $\gamma$ is normal and $\delta$ is regular
semisimple, this implies $h \in T_\gamma$, so
$[\gamma, x, y]$ and $[\gamma', x', y']$ are equivalent
since $[x, y].h = [x', y']$.

\item
Let $\varsigma = \zeta\sigma_{L/E}(\zeta)^{-1}$
and $\varsigma' = \zeta'\sigma_{L/E}(\zeta')^{-1}$.
As in the previous part, $[\zeta, z]$ and
$[\zeta', z']$ have the same invariants if and only
if $[\varsigma, z, z^\ast]$ and
$[\varsigma', z', z'^\ast]$ are in the same $\mathrm{GL}_n(E)$-orbit.

Suppose that 
\[
    [\varsigma, z, z^\ast].g = [\varsigma', z', z'^\ast]
\]
for $g \in \mathrm{GL}_n(E)$. Since $\varsigma\varsigma^\ast
= \varsigma'\varsigma'^\ast$, we have
\begin{align*}
    [\varsigma, z, z^\ast].g^{\ast, -1} 
    &= [g^\ast \varsigma g^{\ast,-1}, zg^{\ast, -1}, g^\ast z^\ast] \\
    &= [g^{-1}\varsigma'^{-1} g, g^{-1} z^\ast, zg]^\ast\\ 
    &= [\varsigma^{-1}, z'^\ast, z']^\ast\\
    &= [\varsigma, z', z'^\ast],
\end{align*}
so $g \in \mathrm{U}(V)$.
Let $h = \zeta^{-1} g \zeta'$. 
We check that  
\[
    \sigma_{L/E}(h) = \sigma_{L/E}(\zeta)^{-1} g \sigma_{L/E}(\zeta')
    = \zeta^{-1} g \zeta' = h,
\]
where the middle equality holds since 
$g^{-1}\varsigma g = \varsigma'$.
Since $g$, $\zeta$, $\zeta' \in \mathrm{U}(V_K)$, we also have
$h \in \mathrm{U}(V)$.
Thus $\zeta = \zeta'$ since $\zeta' = g^{-1}\zeta h$.

Since $\zeta$ is normal and $\varsigma$ is regular
semisimple, we have $g = h \in T_\zeta$, so $[\zeta, z]$
and $[\zeta', z']$ are equivalent since $z' h = z$. 
\qedhere
\end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Lie algebra orbit spaces x and y(V)
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathfrak x = \mathfrak{gl}_n \times F_n \times F^{-,n}$,
and let $\mathfrak y(V) = \mathfrak h(V) \times V^\vee$.
The groups $\mathrm{GL}_n$ and $\mathrm{U}(V)$ act on $\mathfrak x$ and
$\mathfrak y(V)$, respectively, via
\[
    [A, x, y].h = [h^{-1} A h, xh, h^{-1}y],\quad
    [A', z].h = [h^{-1}A' h, zh].
\]
Let $\mathfrak x_{\textnormal{rss}}(F)/\mathrm{GL}_n(F)$ and $\mathfrak y(V)_{\textnormal{rss}}(F)/\mathrm{U}(V)(F)$
denote the regular semisimple orbits of $\mathfrak x(F)$
and $\mathfrak y(V)(F)$ under these actions.
nodes.label: def:lieorbits

nodes.name: Lie algebra orbit matching
nodes.statement:
There is a bijection
\[
    \mathfrak x_{\textnormal{rss}}(F)/\mathrm{GL}_n(F) \simeq \coprod_{V}
    \mathfrak y(V)_{\textnormal{rss}}(F)/\mathrm{U}(V)(F)
\]
such that $[A, x, y]$ and $[A', z]$ match
if and only if $[A, x, y]$ and $[A', z, z^\ast]$
are in the same $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-orbit.
conclusions: There is a bijection \[ \mathfrak x_{\textnormal{rss}}(F)/\mathrm{GL}_n(F) \simeq \coprod_{V} \mathfrak y(V)_{\textnormal{rss}}(F)/\mathrm{U}(V)(F) \]

of $\textnormal{S}_{n,L/K}$ which satisfies

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.4.8
nodes.statement:
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[(1)]
\item First note that $\gamma$ normal implies
$\sigma_{L/M}(\delta) = \delta$. Also, since
$h \in \mathrm{GL}(V)$, it is clear that $\varsigma \in \textnormal{S}_{n, L/E}$.
This combined with $\varsigma \in \mathrm{U}(V)(K)$ implies
$\sigma_{L/E}(\varsigma^\ast) = \varsigma$.

The fact that $\varsigma = \zeta\sigma_{L/E}(\zeta)^{-1}$
and commutes with $\zeta$ is obvious, since
$\sigma_{L/E}(\zeta) = h^{-1}\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma) h$,
so we just
need to check that $\zeta\zeta^\ast = 1$. 
To this end, note that since $\gamma$ is normal,
\[
    \gamma = c_{n-1}\delta^{n-1} + \cdots + c_0
\]
for some $c_0, \dots, c_{n-1} \in L$.
This implies
\[
    \sigma_{L/M}(\gamma) = \sigma_{L/M}(c_{n-1})
    \delta^{n-1} + \cdots + \sigma_{L/M}(c_0),
\]
and
\[
    \zeta = c_{n-1}\varsigma^{n-1} + \cdots + c_0,
\]
since $\zeta = h^{-1}\gamma h$ and $\varsigma = h^{-1}\delta h$.
Note that $\sigma_{L/E}(\varsigma^\ast) = \varsigma$ then implies
\begin{align*}
    \sigma_{L/E}(\zeta^\ast) = \sigma_{L/M}(c_{n-1}) \varsigma^{n-1}
    + \cdots + \sigma_{L/M}(c_0) = h^{-1}\sigma_{L/M}(\gamma) h.
\end{align*}
This implies $\zeta^\ast = h^{-1}\sigma_{L/K}(\gamma) h$,
so $\zeta\zeta^\ast = 1$ since
$\gamma\sigma_{L/K}(\gamma) = 1$.

\item As before, we have $\sigma_{L/E}(\varsigma^\ast) = \varsigma$,
and $\delta \in \textnormal{S}_{n, L/E}$, so $\delta_{L/M}(\delta) 
= \delta$. Since $\zeta$ commutes with $\varsigma$,
we have
\[
    \zeta = c_{n-1} \varsigma^{n-1} + \cdots + c_0
\]
for some $c_0, \dots, c_{n-1} \in L$.
Then
\[
    \sigma_{L/E}(\zeta^\ast)
    = \sigma_{L/M}(c_{n-1}) \varsigma^{n-1} + \cdots + 
    \sigma_{L/M}(c_0),
\]
\[
    \gamma = c_{n-1} \delta^{n-1} + \cdots + c_0,
\]
and
\[
    \sigma_{L/M}(\gamma) =
    \sigma_{L/M}(c_{n-1})\delta^{n-1} + \cdots +
    \sigma_{L/M}(c_0)
    = h^{-1}\sigma_{L/E}(\zeta^\ast)h,
\]
which implies 
$\sigma_{L/K}(\gamma) = h^{-1}\zeta^\ast h$,
so $\gamma\sigma_{L/K}(\gamma) = 1$. As before,
it is clear that $\gamma$ is normal
and satisfies $\delta = \gamma\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma)^{-1}$.
\qedhere
\end{enumerate}

satisfies $\alpha \sigma_{M/F}(\alpha) = 1$
and is not an eigenvalue of $\delta = \gamma\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma)^{-1}$
or $\varsigma = \zeta\sigma_{L/E}(\zeta)^{-1}$. 
Then we have
$[j_M c_\alpha(\delta), x, y] \in \mathfrak x_{\textnormal{rss}}(F)$
and $[j_M c_\alpha(\varsigma), z] \in \mathfrak y(V)_{\textnormal{rss}}(F)$.
assumptions: $[\gamma, x, y] \in X_{\textnormal{rss}}$ and $[\zeta, z] \in Y_{\textnormal{rss}}^V$
$\alpha \in M$ satisfies $\alpha \sigma_{M/F}(\alpha) = 1$ and is not an eigenvalue of $\delta = \gamma\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma)^{-1}$ or $\varsigma = \zeta\sigma_{L/E}(\zeta)^{-1}$

nodes.name: Matching of orbits
nodes.statement:
There is a natural bijection 
\[
  [X_{\textnormal{rss}}] \simeq \coprod_{V} [Y_{\textnormal{rss}}^V]
\]
such that $[\gamma, x, y]$ and $[\zeta, z]^V$ match 
if and only if they have the same invariants.
conclusions: There is a natural bijection \[ [X_{\textnormal{rss}}] \simeq \coprod_{V} [Y_{\textnormal{rss}}^V] \] such that $[\gamma, x, y]$ and $[\zeta, z]^V$ match if and only if they have the same invariants.
nodes.statement_short: Regular semisimple classes on the GL side biject with the disjoint union over V of unitary classes, matched by invariants.
nodes.label: lem:matching

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.4.10
nodes.statement:
As usual, we let 
$\delta = \gamma\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma)^{-1}$, and
$\varsigma = \zeta\sigma_{L/E}(\zeta)^{-1}$.
Note that $[\gamma, x, y]$ and $[\zeta, z]$
have the same invariants if and only if
$[\delta, x, y]$ and $[\varsigma, z, z^\ast]$ 
are in the same $\mathrm{GL}(V)$-orbit, which is true
if and only if for any $\alpha$
as in Lemma \ref{lem:rsscayley},
$[j_M c_\alpha(\delta), x, y] \in \mathfrak x_{\textnormal{rss}}(F)$ and 
$[j_M c_\alpha(\varsigma), z] \in \mathfrak y(V)_{\textnormal{rss}}(F)$ 
match in the sense of Lemma \ref{lem:liematch}.
Thus the proposition follows from Lemmas \ref{lem:embed},
\ref{lem:liematch}, 
\ref{lem:normmatch}, and \ref{lem:rsscayley}.

Indeed, suppose $[\gamma, x, y] \in X_{\textnormal{rss}}$.
Let $\alpha \in M$ be as in Lemma \ref{lem:rsscayley}.
By Lemma \ref{lem:liematch}, there exists
$[A', z'] \in \mathfrak y(V)_{\textnormal{rss}}(F)$, for a unique $V$, such
that 
\[
    [j_M c_\alpha(\delta), x, y].h =
    [A', z', z'^\ast]
\]
for some $h \in \mathrm{GL}(V)$.
Let $\varsigma = c_\alpha^{-1}(j_M^{-1} A')$.
Then $\varsigma = h^{-1}\delta h$, so by Lemma
\ref{lem:normmatch}, we have $\varsigma = 
\zeta\sigma_{L/E}(\zeta)^{-1}$ for some $\zeta'
\in \mathrm{U}(V)(K)$. Suppose 
$\zeta' = h_1^{-1}\zeta h_2$ for $\zeta \in R^V$
and $h_1, h_2 \in \mathrm{U}(V)(F)$.
Let $z = z' h_1^{-1}$.
Then $[\zeta, z] \in Y_{\textnormal{rss}}^V$, and $[\zeta, z]$
and $[\gamma, x, y]$ 
have the same invariants.
Furthermore, $[\zeta, z] \in Y_{\textnormal{rss}}^V$ is unique by Lemma
\ref{lem:embed}.

The same argument shows that for any $[\zeta, z]
\in Y_{\textnormal{rss}}^V$, there exists a unique $[\gamma, x, y]
\in X_{\textnormal{rss}}$ such that $[\gamma, x, y]$ and
$[\zeta, z]$ have the same invariants.
nodes.statement_short: Cayley-transform norms to the Lie algebra, use Zhang's Lie-algebra matching, and lift back with Lemma 2.4.8; uniqueness from Lemma 2.4.5.

nodes.statement:

nodes.name: Criterion for an orbit to contain a normal element
nodes.statement:
Let $\zeta \in \mathrm{U}(V)(K)$ be an element which
is regular semisimple with respect to the 
$\mathrm{U}(V)(F) \times \mathrm{U}(V)(F)$ action. The orbit
$\mathrm{U}(V)(F) \zeta \mathrm{U}(V)(F)$ contains a normal element if and
only if
\[
    \zeta\sigma_{L/E}(\zeta)^{-1}
    = \gamma\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma)^{-1}
\]
for some $\gamma \in \textnormal{S}_{n, L/K}$.
assumptions: Let $\zeta \in \mathrm{U}(V)(K)$ be an element which is regular semisimple with respect to the $\mathrm{U}(V)(F) \times \mathrm{U}(V)(F)$ action.
conclusions: The orbit $\mathrm{U}(V)(F) \zeta \mathrm{U}(V)(F)$ contains a normal element if and only if \[ \zeta\sigma_{L/E}(\zeta)^{-1} = \gamma\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma)^{-1} \] for some $\gamma \in \textnormal{S}_{n, L/K}$.
equivalent_conditions: The orbit $\mathrm{U}(V)(F) \zeta \mathrm{U}(V)(F)$ contains a normal element
nodes.label: lem:unitarynormalexistence

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.4.11
nodes.statement:
Suppose $h_1^{-1} \zeta h_2$ is normal for some
$h_1, h_2 \in \mathrm{U}(V)(F)$. By
Proposition \ref{lem:matching}, there exists
$\gamma' \in \textnormal{S}_{n, L/K}$ such that
\[
    h_1^{-1}\zeta\sigma_{L/E}(\zeta) h_1^{-1}
    = h^{-1}\gamma'\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma')^{-1} h
\]
for some $h \in \mathrm{GL}_n(E)$.
This is equivalent to $\zeta\sigma_{L/E}(\zeta)^{-1}
= \gamma\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma)^{-1}$ for
$\gamma = h_1 h^{-1}\gamma' \sigma_{E/F}(h h_1^{-1})$.

On the other hand, suppose that we are given
$\zeta\sigma_{L/E}(\zeta)^{-1} =
\gamma\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma)^{-1}$ for $\gamma
\in \textnormal{S}_{n, L/K}$. 
By Proposition \ref{prop:normalrep}, there exists
$h \in \mathrm{GL}_n(E)$ such that $h^{-1}\gamma
\sigma_{E/F}(h)$ is normal. 
Then by Lemma \ref{lem:normmatch} (1), there exists
normal $\zeta' \in \mathrm{U}(V)(K)$ with
$\zeta'\sigma_{L/E}(\zeta')^{-1}
= \zeta\sigma_{L/E}(\zeta)^{-1}$, which implies
that $\zeta'$ is in the orbit $\mathrm{U}(V)(F)\zeta \mathrm{U}(V)(F)$.
nodes.statement_short: Forward via orbit matching; converse via existence of normal representatives and Lemma 2.4.8(1).

nodes.name: If the orbit has a normal element, matching gives gamma with
nodes.statement:

Proposition \ref{lem:matching}, there exists

\[
    h_1^{-1}\zeta\sigma_{L/E}(\zeta) h_1^{-1}
    = h^{-1}\gamma'\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma')^{-1} h
\]
for some $h \in \mathrm{GL}_n(E)$.
This is equivalent to $\zeta\sigma_{L/E}(\zeta)^{-1}
= \gamma\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma)^{-1}$ for
$\gamma = h_1 h^{-1}\gamma' \sigma_{E/F}(h h_1^{-1})$.
nodes.statement_short: If the orbit has a normal element, matching gives gamma with the same norm.

nodes.name: Conversely, a gamma with the same norm yields a normal zeta'
nodes.statement:
On the other hand, suppose that we are given
$\zeta\sigma_{L/E}(\zeta)^{-1} =
\gamma\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma)^{-1}$ for $\gamma
\in \textnormal{S}_{n, L/K}$. 
By Proposition \ref{prop:normalrep}, there exists
$h \in \mathrm{GL}_n(E)$ such that $h^{-1}\gamma
\sigma_{E/F}(h)$ is normal. 
Then by Lemma \ref{lem:normmatch} (1), there exists
normal $\zeta' \in \mathrm{U}(V)(K)$ with
$\zeta'\sigma_{L/E}(\zeta')^{-1}
= \zeta\sigma_{L/E}(\zeta)^{-1}$, which implies
that $\zeta'$ is in the orbit $\mathrm{U}(V)(F)\zeta \mathrm{U}(V)(F)$.
nodes.statement_short: Conversely, a gamma with the same norm yields a normal zeta' in the orbit.

nodes.name: Local-global principle for norms times F^x
nodes.statement:
Let $M/F$ and $K/F$ be quadratic extensions of number
fields. Let $L = M \otimes_F K$.
Let $N_{L/M} \colon L \to M$ and
$N_{L_v/M_v} \colon L_v \to M_v$ denote the norm maps. 
Let $x \in M^\times$ be such that
\[
    x \in N_{L_v/M_v}(L_v^\times) \cdot F_v^\times
\]
for all places $v$ of $F$. Then
$x \in N_{L/M}(L^\times)\cdot F^\times$.
assumptions: Let $M/F$ and $K/F$ be quadratic extensions of number fields.
conclusions: $x \in N_{L/M}(L^\times)\cdot F^\times$
nodes.label: lem:normtimesF

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.4.12
nodes.statement:
The assumption on $x$ tells us that there exists
$(f_v)_v \in \mathbb A^\times$ such that
$x \cdot (f_v)_v \in N_{L/M}(\mathbb A_L^\times)$.
Since $x \in M$, we have
\[
    \eta_{K/F}((f_v)_v) = \eta_{L/M}(x) = 1,
\]
where $\eta_{K/F} \colon \mathbb A^\times/F^\times
\to \mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$ and
$\eta_{L/M} \colon \mathbb A_M^\times/M^\times
\to \mathrm{Gal}(L/M)$
are the maps coming from global class field theory.
Since the kernel of $\eta_{K/F}$ is 
$N_{K/F}(\mathbb A_K^\times)$,
there exists $f \in F^\times$ such that
\[
    f^{-1} \cdot (f_v)_v \in N_{K/F}(\mathbb A_K^\times)
    \subseteq N_{L/M}(\mathbb A_L^\times).
\]
This means that $xf \in N_{L/M}(\mathbb A_L^\times)$,
and since $xf \in M$, by the Hasse norm
theorem, this implies that $xf \in N_{L/M}(L^\times)$.
nodes.statement_short: Use class field theory to adjust the idelic factor by a global f in F^x, then apply the Hasse norm theorem.

\]

nodes.statement:
This means that $xf \in N_{L/M}(\mathbb A_L^\times)$,

nodes.statement_short: By the Hasse norm theorem xf is a global norm.

nodes.name: Local-global principle for normal orbits
nodes.statement:
Suppose $\delta \in \textnormal{S}_{n, M/F} \coloneqq
\textnormal{S}_{n,L/K} \cap \mathrm{GL}_n(M)$ is regular semisimple.
Then $\delta = \gamma\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma)^{-1}$
for some $\gamma \in \textnormal{S}_{n, L/K}$ if and only
if $\delta = \gamma_v\sigma_{L_v/E_v}(\gamma_v)^{-1}$
for some $\gamma_v \in \textnormal{S}_{n, L_v/K_v}$, for every
place $v$ of $F$.
conclusions: $\delta = \gamma\sigma_{L/E}(\gamma)^{-1}$ for some $\gamma \in \textnormal{S}_{n, L/K}$ if and only if $\delta = \gamma_v\sigma_{L_v/E_v}(\gamma_v)^{-1}$ for some $\gamma_v \in \textnormal{S}_{n, L_v/K_v}$, for every place $v$ of $F$
equivalent_conditions: $\delta = \gamma_v\sigma_{L_v/E_v}(\gamma_v)^{-1}$ for some $\gamma_v \in \textnormal{S}_{n, L_v/K_v}$, for every place $v$ of $F$
nodes.label: lem:localglobal

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.4.13
nodes.statement:
Let $L'$ be the centralizer of $\delta$ in
$\mathrm{Mat}_n(L)$, and let $M'$ be the centralizer of
$\delta$ in $\mathrm{Mat}_n(M)$. 
Since $\delta\sigma_{M/F}(\delta) = 1$, we have
that $\sigma_{M/F}$ acts on $M'$ and 
$\sigma_{L/K}$ and $\sigma_{L/E}$ act on $L'$. 
Let $F'$ be the
$\sigma_{M/F}$-fixed elements of $M'$, and let
$K'$ and $E'$ be the $\sigma_{L/K}$-fixed and
$\sigma_{L/E}$-fixed elements of $L'$.

Recall from Lemma \ref{lem:normalequivdefs} that
if $\gamma_v\sigma_{L_v/E_v}(\gamma_v)^{-1} =
\delta$ for $\gamma_v \in \textnormal{S}_{n, L_v/K_v}$, then
$\gamma_v$ is normal, so $\gamma_v \in L_v'$.
Thus, we are given that
\[
    \delta = \gamma_v\sigma_{L_v'/E_v'}(\gamma_v)^{-1}
\]
for some $\gamma_v \in L_v'$ with
$\gamma_v\sigma_{L_v'/K_v'}(\gamma_v) = 1$
for each place $v$ of $F$, and we want to show
that $\delta = \gamma\sigma_{L'/E'}(\gamma)^{-1}$
for some $\gamma \in L'$ with
$\gamma\sigma_{L'/K'}(\gamma) = 1$.

Since $\delta$ is regular semisimple, $F'$ is a product
of field extensions on $F$, and
it clearly suffices to prove the claim in the case 
that $F'$ is a field.

Then since $\delta\sigma_{M'/F'}(\delta) = 1$, there exists
$x \in M'$ such that $\delta = x\sigma_{M'/F'}(x)^{-1}$.
Since $\gamma_v\sigma_{L_v'/K_v'}(\gamma_v) = 1$, 
there exists $\xi_v \in L_v'$ such that
$\gamma_v = \xi_v\sigma_{L_v'/K_v'}(\xi_v)^{-1}$, so
\[
    x\sigma_{M'/F'}(x)^{-1} = \delta
    = \gamma_v\sigma_{L_v'/E_v'}(\gamma_v)^{-1}
    = \xi_v\sigma_{L_v'/K_v'}(\xi_v)^{-1}
    \sigma_{L_v'/M_v'}(\xi_v)\sigma_{L_v'/E_v'}(\xi_v)^{-1}.
\]
This implies that $x \in \xi_v\sigma_{L_v'/M_v'}(\xi_v)
\cdot F_v'^\times$, so 
\[ 
    x \in N_{L_v'/M_v'}(L_v'^\times) \cdot F_v'^\times
\]
for all places $v$ of $F$.
Then by Lemma \ref{lem:normtimesF},  
$x \in N_{L'/M'}(L'^\times) \cdot F'^\times$. 
Thus, there exists $\xi \in L'^\times$ and $f \in F'^\times$
such that $x = \xi\sigma_{L'/M'}(\xi) f$. 
Then, if we let $\gamma = \xi\sigma_{L'/K'}(\xi)^{-1}$,
we have
\[
    \delta = x\sigma_{M'/F'}(x)^{-1}
    = \xi\sigma_{L'/M'}(\xi)\sigma_{L'/E'}(\xi)^{-1}
    \sigma_{L'/K'}(\xi)^{-1}
    = \gamma\sigma_{L'/E'}(\gamma)^{-1}.
    \qedhere
\]
nodes.statement_short: Pass to the centralizer algebras of delta, reduce to a field, and apply Lemma 2.4.12 (Hasse norm) to globalize the local solutions.

Since $\delta$ is regular semisimple, $F'$ is a product
